rationale: Both prefer a modest meal with peace or friendship to abundant food accompanied by hostility; 17:1 contrasts its pleasant morsel with a house of unjust sacrifices and battle.
The intelligent servant's rule over foolish masters in 17:2 corresponds to the fool serving the intelligent person in 11:29; the former also describes his division of the brothers' portions.
Proverbs places the testing of silver and gold beside hearts chosen before the Lord; Wisdom describes God testing and accepting the righteous like gold in a crucible.
The righteous person who ignores lying lips in 17:4 corresponds to the righteous person's hatred of an unjust word in 13:5, contrasting with evil attention to lawless speech.
Mocking the poor in 17:5 and extorting the needy in 14:31 both provoke their Maker; each saying connects reverence for God with treatment of the poor.
The final promise that the compassionate will receive mercy corresponds to Jesus' blessing of the merciful because they will receive mercy.
Both present grandchildren as a benefit to the older man: a crown in 17:6 and an inheritance in 13:22.

The proverb assigns the whole world's possessions to the faithful; Paul tells those belonging to Christ that the world and all things are theirs. These are related claims of belonging, without an explicit quotation claim.
The claim that lying lips do not suit the righteous corresponds to 12:22's rejection of lying lips before the Lord and approval of faithful deeds.
Discipline brings a reward of favors and prosperity to its users in 17:8; 13:18 likewise connects discipline and acceptance of rebukes with escape from dishonor and receipt of glory.
Proverbs 17:9 connects handling an injustice with preserving or separating friends; 16:28 explicitly attributes the separation of friends to the crooked man's deceitful activity.
The fool who fails to perceive even when whipped in 17:10 corresponds to the fool whose foolishness remains despite public whipping in 27:22.
Proverbs 17:11 threatens a dispute-maker with the Lord's merciless messenger; 16:14 pictures a king's wrath as a messenger of death. Both use a punitive messenger image, with different senders.
The proverb condemns repaying good with evil; the psalmist complains that his opponents exchanged his good deeds for evils and his love for hatred.
The proverb rejects both acquitting the unjust and condemning the righteous; Exodus forbids unrighteous charges, killing the innocent or righteous, and justifying the ungodly for gifts.
Proverbs 17:16 denies that a fool's wealth enables him to acquire wisdom; 14:6 likewise says wisdom will not be found among evil people, contrasting the discernment available among the intelligent.
The warning that turning crookedly away from learning brings evils corresponds to 15:10's warning that those who hate rebukes die shamefully.
The enduring friend and the brother useful in need in 17:17 can be read with 27:10's counsel to keep one's friend and its preference for a nearby friend over a distant brother in misfortune.
The guarantor's pledge for a friend in 17:18 corresponds to the guarantee in 6:1-3, which describes giving one's hand over to an enemy, entrapment by one's own lips and the need to seek release.
Proverbs 17:19 joins love of sin to delight in battles; 29:22 likewise connects wrath with digging up strife and anger with digging out sins.
The hard-hearted person who fails to meet good in 17:20 corresponds to the hard-hearted person who falls into evils in 28:14.
The foolish son brings his father no joy in 17:21, while an intelligent son gladdens his mother; 10:1 also contrasts the wise son's parental joy with the foolish son's parental grief.
Both describe the heart's emotional condition through bodily effects: joy produces flourishing, while sorrow produces gloom in 15:13 and dried bones in 17:22.
The drying of a sorrowful man's bones contrasts with the good report that makes bones full; both sayings also connect good experiences with a glad or flourishing heart.
Gifts taken unjustly in a person's lap and the bending of righteous ways correspond to Exodus's warning that received gifts blind the seeing and corrupt righteous words.
The ways of someone taking gifts unjustly do not prosper in 17:23; 15:27 likewise warns that taking bribes destroys their recipient.
The foolish son's anger for his father and pain for his mother develop the family grief attributed to a foolish son in 10:1.
The prohibition on penalizing the righteous and plotting against righteous rulers shares Exodus's protection of the innocent and righteous from an unjust charge and killing.
Both explicitly connect patience with understanding: 17:27 associates restraint from harsh words with discernment, while 14:29 calls the patient man great in understanding.
Avoiding a harsh word in 17:27 accords with 15:1's contrast between the yielding answer that turns wrath away and the painful word that stirs anger.
Proverbs 11:12 associates intelligence with keeping quiet; 17:28 says that making oneself mute makes one appear intelligent.
The person who separates from friends seeks pretexts and invites reproach in 18:1; 27:10 gives the opposing instruction not to abandon one's friend or ancestral friend.
The fool who has no use for wisdom in 18:2 corresponds to the person called foolish for hating rebukes in 12:1, in contrast to love for discipline and discernment.
Both compare content of a man's heart to deep water; 18:4 describes a word and the springing of a river and fountain, while 20:5 describes counsel drawn out by an intelligent man.
Admiring the impious person's face and perverting judgment in 18:5 corresponds to the declaration in 24:23 that deference to a face in judgment is not good.
The rash mouth that calls for death in 18:6 corresponds to the rash person's mouth drawing near to ruin in 10:14.
The fool's lips trap his life in 18:7; in 12:13 the sinner falls into traps through the sin of his lips. Both connect harmful speech with danger to its speaker.
Both sayings associate disabling fear or cowardice with idleness and hunger; 18:8's hunger statement corresponds to 19:15's explicit warning that the idle person's life will hunger.
Running to the strength of the Lord's name and being raised high corresponds to the psalmist being raised upon a rock and calling God a tower of strength before the enemy.
Both expressly picture the rich person's possessions as a fortified city; 18:11 adds the image of a great shadow to this portrayal of wealth as security.
The heart's pride before ruin in 18:12 corresponds to insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall in 16:18.
Both pair pride or insolence bringing a person low with humility leading to glory; 29:23 expressly identifies the Lord as supporting the humble-minded.
Answering before hearing is called folly in Proverbs; James gives the corresponding positive counsel to be quick to hear and slow to speak.

The intelligent attendant who calms anger in 18:14 corresponds to the gentle-tempered man called a physician of the heart in 14:30. Both describe another person's temperate care as relieving distress.
The intelligent heart acquiring discernment in 18:15 repeats the association between an upright heart and seeking discernment in 15:14.

A gift makes room for its giver and seats him with rulers in 18:16; 25:6-7 distinguishes being invited upward from presumptuously taking a ruler's place. Both concern access and seating before rulers.
Proverbs describes a lot making a determination among rulers; Acts records a lot determining which proposed man would take the vacant place among the apostles after prayer.
The brother helped by a brother is compared to a fortified city in 18:19; 17:17 identifies brothers as useful in need. Each describes the practical security of mutual kinship aid.
Both describe filling from the fruit of mouth or lips; 18:20 names a filled belly, while 12:14 speaks of good things filling the life and of recompense from the lips.
The tongue's power over death and life in 18:21 corresponds to 12:18's contrast between speech that wounds like a sword and the wise tongue that heals.
Finding a good wife brings favor and gladness from God in 18:22; 19:14 attributes the joining of wife and husband to God, distinguishing it from inherited possessions.
Casting out a good wife and retaining an adulteress is condemned in 18:22a; 5:18-20 instead urges delight in the wife of one's youth and rejects embracing another woman.
The person whose own folly ruins his ways nevertheless blames God in Proverbs; James rejects blaming God for temptation and traces temptation and sin to one's own desire.
Both contrast the many friends associated with wealth against the abandonment or hatred experienced by a poor friend.
Proverbs warns that a false witness and unjust accuser will not escape; Exodus forbids receiving an empty report or agreeing with the unrighteous to become an unrighteous witness.
The many who attend kings' faces in 19:6 correspond to the many who court leaders' faces in 29:26; the latter adds that a person's justice comes from the Lord.
The opening description of hatred toward a poor brother and estrangement from friendship corresponds to the hatred experienced by poor friends in 14:20.
Acquiring and preserving understanding is described as loving oneself in 19:8; 15:32 likewise describes keeping rebukes as loving one's own life, against rejecting discipline.
The keeper of understanding who finds good things in 19:8 corresponds to the understanding person explicitly called a finder of good things in 16:20.
Both sayings begin with the warning that a false witness will not go unpunished; their second clauses develop the destructive outcome of wrongful accusation or kindled wickedness.
The fool's inappropriate luxury and the servant's insolent rule in 19:10 correspond to the unsettling examples of a fool filled with food and a household servant becoming king in 30:21-23.
The merciful person's patience in 19:11 corresponds to love described together as patient and kind in 1 Corinthians; the link concerns those joined qualities.
Both compare a king's threatening power to a lion; 19:12 also contrasts that threat with his cheerfulness like dew, while 20:2 stresses the danger of provoking him.
The foolish son who brings shame to his father in 19:13 corresponds to the foolish son's parental grief in 10:1; the connection concerns the first clause of 19:13.
Proverbs calls prayers associated with a courtesan's fee impure; Deuteronomy forbids bringing a prostitute's hire into the Lord's house for a vow.
God's joining of wife and husband in 19:14 corresponds to the favor and gladness from God associated with finding a good wife in 18:22.
The connection of cowardice, idleness and hunger in 19:15 corresponds to the disabling fear and hunger associated with the lazy in 18:8.
Keeping the command guards one's life in 19:16, while despising one's ways brings death; 16:17 similarly joins disciplined, righteous ways and guarding one's ways to preservation of life.
Showing mercy to the poor is a loan God will repay in 19:17; 28:27 similarly promises that one who gives to the poor will not be in need.
The instruction to discipline a son so that he will be hopeful corresponds to the careful discipline attributed to a parent's love in 13:24.
The command to listen to a father's discipline so as to become wise in later days corresponds to 4:1's appeal to children to hear paternal discipline and attend to understanding.
Human reasonings are many but the Lord's counsel endures in 19:21; 21:1 pictures even a king's heart in God's hand and inclined wherever He wills.
The righteous poor person is preferred to a rich liar in 19:22, corresponding to 28:6's preference for a poor person walking in truth over a lying rich person.

relationship: fear of the Lord and life
rationale: The fear of the Lord is directed toward life in 19:23; 10:27 similarly says that it adds days, in contrast to the shortened years of the impious.
Both portray hands hidden in a lap and failure to bring them to the mouth. Proverbs 19:24 calls the hiding unjust, while 26:15 assigns the image to a lazy person.
Both describe an undisciplined or pestilent person's punishment teaching an observer, and then contrast the knowledge received by an intelligent or wise person.
The child who dishonors his father and thrusts away his mother corresponds to the one who casts away father or mother while denying the sin in 28:24.
Neglecting a father's discipline leads to meditation on evil sayings in 19:27; 15:5 similarly identifies sneering at a father's discipline with foolishness.
Both criticize taking on a guarantee: 19:28 calls guaranteeing a foolish child insolence toward just judgment, while 17:18 compares a friend's guarantor with a foolish man's self-rejoicing.
Whips and punishments are assigned to the undisciplined and fools in 19:29; 26:3 compares a rod for a lawless nation to the whip and goad used for animals.
Proverbs opposes drunken insolence to wisdom; Ephesians joins its warning against foolishness to a command against drunkenness with wine and its reckless excess.
Both depict a king's threat as a lion's wrath or growling; 20:2 explicitly warns that provoking this threat endangers one's life.
Turning away from abuse brings glory in 20:3, while a fool becomes entangled in it; 15:18 similarly contrasts a patient person's calming of battle with a quick-tempered person's creation of it.
Both picture something within a person's heart as deep water: counsel drawn out by an intelligent man in 20:5, and a word that becomes a river and fountain in 18:4.

The difficulty of finding a faithful man corresponds to the psalm's lament that truths have become few and neighbors speak deceitfully. The proverb's praise of humanity and mercy remains its own setting.
The blameless person's righteousness leaves his children blessed in 20:7; 14:26 similarly connects fear of the Lord with leaving support for one's children.
The righteous king before whom no evil stands in 20:8 corresponds to 25:5's removal of impious people from before a king so that his throne prospers in righteousness.
The challenge to boast of a pure heart or freedom from sins corresponds to Solomon's acknowledgement that there is no person who will not sin.
Both link dishonoring parents with a judgment pictured through the eyes: darkness in 20:9a, and the mocking eye being pecked out in 30:17.
An eagerly pursued portion ends without blessing in 20:9b; 13:11 likewise warns that eagerly pursued property becomes less, specifically describing that pursuit as lawless.
Proverbs forbids saying one will punish the enemy and directs waiting for the Lord's help; Romans similarly forbids self-avenging and reserves repayment to the Lord.
The rejection of unequal weights and double measures before the Lord corresponds to 11:1's rejection of deceitful scales and approval of a just weight.
In the context of 20:10's false measures, their maker is fettered in his practices; 5:22 similarly pictures a man bound tightly by the cords of his own sins.
The ear and eye are both works of the Lord in Proverbs; the psalm argues from God's planting of the ear and forming of the eye that He hears and perceives.
The warning against speaking against others lest one be cut off corresponds to 13:3's connection between guarding one's mouth and preserving one's life.
Both condemn deceitful scales before the Lord; 20:23 also explicitly names the double weight as an abomination.
A person's steps directed by the Lord in 20:24 correspond to the steps set right by God in 15:29b, where the heart is told to consider righteous things.
The trap of consecrating something quickly and regretting the vow corresponds to Ecclesiastes' counsel to pay what one vows and its preference for not vowing over vowing without payment.
The wise king's winnowing of the impious corresponds to 25:5's removal of the impious from before a king so that his throne prospers in righteousness.

relationship: divine scrutiny of the inward person
rationale: Proverbs describes the Lord searching the belly's inward chambers; Jeremiah similarly has the Lord examine hearts and test kidneys before giving each person according to his ways.
Mercy and truth surround the king's throne in righteousness in 20:28; 29:14 likewise connects the establishment of his throne with judging the poor in truth.
Gray hair as the elders' glory corresponds to old age as a crown of boasting in 16:31; the link concerns the elderly, while 20:29 separately praises young men's wisdom.
The bruises, wounds and blows assigned to evil people in 20:30 correspond to the whips and punishments prepared for the undisciplined and fools in 19:29.
The proverb pictures a king's heart inclined by God; Ezra gives a narrative example when the Lord stirs Cyrus's spirit and the king announces the commission to build God's house.
A person appearing righteous to himself in 21:2 corresponds to fools' ways appearing upright before them in 12:15, which contrasts that self-assessment with listening to counsel.
Proverbs contrasts human self-approval with the Lord setting hearts straight; Jeremiah contrasts the heart's depth beyond human knowledge with the Lord examining it and judging its ways.
Both expressly place doing righteous things above offering sacrifices in God's estimation; 21:3 additionally names speaking truth and the blood of sacrifices.
The insolent, lofty-minded and rash-hearted person in 21:4 corresponds to the high-hearted person declared unclean before God in 16:5.
Accumulating stores through a false tongue leads toward emptiness and death traps in 21:6; 13:11 likewise warns that property eagerly pursued with lawlessness diminishes.
Destruction comes upon those unwilling to do righteous things in 21:7; 11:6 similarly describes lawless people caught in their own destruction, in contrast to the rescue righteousness brings.
God sends crooked ways to crooked people while His works remain upright; the psalm similarly describes God's dealings corresponding to the holy, innocent, chosen and twisted person.
Both prefer an exposed corner to a shared house: 21:9 contrasts its corner with injustice in plastered rooms, while 25:24 contrasts a roof corner with an abusive wife.
Both describe another person's punishment instructing an observer, then contrast this with the knowledge an intelligent or wise person receives through understanding or reproof.
Closing one's ears to the weak results in an unanswered call in 21:13; turning one's eye away from the poor results in great difficulty in 28:27.
The gift that overturns anger in Proverbs corresponds to Jacob's stated hope that gifts sent before him will appease Esau and lead Esau to accept him.
The devout person regarded as unclean by evildoers in 21:15 corresponds to the straightening way regarded as an abomination by the lawless in 29:27.
Leaving righteousness leads to rest among the giants in 21:16; 2:18 places the house of personified evil counsel, identified in 2:17, beside death and its courses beside Hades with the earthborn.
The lawless person as a cleansing-offering for the righteous in 21:18 corresponds to the impious person handed over in the righteous person's place after the righteous escapes in 11:8.
Both prefer an uncomfortable dwelling to hostile company: 21:19 contrasts desert land with a battling, quick-tempered woman, while 25:24 contrasts a roof corner with an abusive wife.
Treasure resting upon the wise person's mouth corresponds to the righteous tongue pictured as fire-tested silver in 10:20. Both give speech a precious-material image.
The way of righteousness and mercy finding life in 21:21 corresponds to the explicit statement in 12:28 that life is in ways of righteousness.

Proverbs describes wisdom overcoming fortified cities; Ecclesiastes describes a wise man delivering a besieged city and judges wisdom better than strength and weapons. The military outcomes differ, but both elevate wisdom over force.
Both directly connect guarding one's mouth with keeping one's life; 21:23 adds the tongue and specifies preservation from affliction.
The person who remembers wrongs is called lawless in 21:24; 12:28 assigns the ways of those who remember wrongs to death, against the life of righteousness.
The lazy person's killing desires and unwilling hands correspond to 13:4's idle person amid desires, contrasted there with courageous hands engaged in care.
The righteous person's unsparing mercy and compassion correspond to the righteous showing compassion and mercy in 13:9a, in contrast to deceitful wandering in sin.
Both explicitly call the sacrifices of the impious an abomination to the Lord; 21:27 gives their lawless manner of offering as the reason.
The false witness who perishes in 21:28 corresponds to 19:9's warning that a false witness will not escape punishment and that kindled wickedness consumes its instigator.
The upright person's understanding of his ways in 21:29 corresponds to the resourceful person's wisdom recognizing his ways in 14:8.
The absence of wisdom and counsel with the impious corresponds to seeking wisdom among evil people and not finding it in 14:6.

The prepared warhorse is distinguished from help that comes from the Lord in Proverbs; the psalm contrasts reliance on horses and chariots with the Lord's name, followed by falling or being raised upright.
Proverbs prefers a good name to much wealth and favor to precious metals; Ecclesiastes similarly ranks a name above good oil.
The proverb says God made both rich and poor; Job appeals to shared formation in the womb when considering his servants' legal case. Both set differences of status beside common human origin.
The resourceful observer instructed by an evil person's punishment corresponds to the fool made more resourceful by watching a pestilent person whipped in 19:25.
Wisdom's offspring include wealth, glory and life in 22:4; 3:16 likewise places length of life, wealth and glory with wisdom.
Avoiding the thistles and traps of crooked ways preserves life in 22:5; 16:17 similarly connects turning from evil and guarding one's ways with keeping one's life.
Sowing worthless things and reaping evils corresponds to Paul's principle that a person reaps what he sows, illustrated by corruption reaped from sowing to the flesh.
God's blessing of the cheerful giving man corresponds closely to Paul's description of God loving a cheerful giver, alongside his rejection of sorrowful or compelled giving.
The person who shared loaves with the poor is promised nourishment in 22:9; 28:27 similarly promises that giving to the poor will not leave the giver in need.

Proverbs 22:9a says the giver takes away the life of those possessing the gifts; 15:27 similarly connects taking bribes with the recipient's destruction, although 22:9a also describes honor for the giver.
Expelling a pestilent council member sends strife away in 22:10; 26:20 likewise says battle becomes quiet where the double-minded person is absent, using firewood as its analogy.
The Lord's love of devout hearts and acceptance of the blameless correspond to 11:20's acceptance before Him of those blameless in their ways.
Both put the excuse of a lion in the roads in the lazy person's mouth; 22:13 adds murderers in the squares.
The lawless person's mouth is a deep pit into which someone falls in 22:14; 11:9 similarly places a trap for citizens in the impious person's mouth.
The command to turn from a crooked and evil way in 22:14a corresponds to 4:27's instruction to turn one's foot away from an evil way.

Proverbs 22:15 puts a young person's attached senselessness beside the distance of rod and discipline; 29:15 conversely assigns wisdom to blows and reproofs and describes the shame of a wandering child.
Both describe extortion from the poor: 22:16 describes the extorter's increased goods and losses in giving to the rich, while 28:3 identifies extortion as the practice of an impious man.
Both direct the learner to apply the ear to the teacher's words and connect this hearing with the heart: understanding their goodness in 22:17 and retaining them in 4:21.
Putting the wise words into the heart in 22:18 corresponds to writing commands on the breadth of the heart in 7:3; 22:18 adds their glad expression upon the lips.
Hope in the Lord corresponds to 3:5's command to trust God with one's whole heart and not exalt oneself in one's own wisdom.
The direction to copy the teachings threefold for counsel and knowledge upon the heart corresponds to 7:3's instruction to write the commands on the breadth of one's heart.
The teacher supplies true words and knowledge so the learner can answer questioners truthfully; Colossians similarly connects cultivated gracious speech with knowing how to answer each person.

relationship: protection of the poor in judgment
rationale: The prohibition on using force against the needy and dishonoring the weak at the gates corresponds to Exodus's prohibition on perverting a poor person's judgment in his case.
The Lord judging the poor person's case corresponds to the mighty Lord who redeems the orphans and judges their case in 23:11.
The warning against lodging with an angry friend can be read with 15:18's explanation that a quick-tempered man prepares battles, unlike the patient person who calms them.
The danger of learning an angry companion's ways corresponds to Sirach's warning that one who associates with a proud person becomes like him, illustrated by touching staining pitch.
The warning against giving oneself as a pledge corresponds to the son's guarantee in 6:1-3, giving his hand over to an enemy, entrapment by his own lips and the command to seek release.
Proverbs warns that inability to pay can cost the debtor his bedding; Exodus requires a pledged garment to be returned before sunset because it is the person's only covering for sleep.
Both forbid moving the boundaries set by one's fathers; Deuteronomy places this protection in the context of the allotted inheritance in the land.
The perceptive worker standing beside kings corresponds to the intelligent attendant acceptable to a king and removing dishonor by skill in 14:35.
Thoughtfully considering the food at rulers' tables corresponds to Sirach's instruction to consider matters at a great table and eat what is set before one without greedy grasping.
The warning not to desire a ruler's food out of insatiability corresponds to Sirach's instruction not to chew greedily and to stop for discipline rather than become insatiable.

Proverbs tells the poor person not to stretch himself to match the rich; Sirach similarly warns against a burden beyond oneself and association with someone stronger and richer, using unequal pots as an image.
Avoiding the begrudging host's desirable food corresponds to the preference in 15:17 for vegetables with friendship over calves with enmity.
The fool's sneering at intelligent words corresponds to the uneducated person's refusal to love a reprover or associate with the wise in 15:12.

The prohibition on moving everlasting boundaries corresponds to Deuteronomy's prohibition on removing ancestral boundaries of the allotted inheritance; Proverbs also specifically protects orphans' property.
The mighty Lord who redeems orphans and judges their case corresponds to the Lord judging the poor person's case in 22:23.

relationship: heart and ear applied to wisdom
rationale: Both combine giving the heart to instruction or understanding with preparing or applying the ear to wisdom and discernment.
The instruction not to refrain from disciplining a child with a rod corresponds to 13:24's contrast between sparing the staff and the careful discipline associated with parental love.
The rod is presented as rescuing the child's life in 23:14; 13:24 likewise presents careful discipline with the staff as an expression of love for one's son.
The child's wise heart gladdening the speaker's heart corresponds to 27:11's direct appeal that the son become wise so the parent's heart may rejoice.
Both directly prohibit envy of evil people or sinners; 23:17 contrasts this with continual fear of the Lord, while 24:1 also rejects desire for their company.
The promise that hope will not depart when the prior instruction is kept corresponds to 24:14's promise that finding wisdom brings a good end and hope that does not abandon the learner.
Both directly address the son and command listening so that he may become wise; 23:19 also calls for straightened reflections, while 19:20 looks to wisdom in later days.

The warning against becoming a wine-drinker can be read with Paul's prohibition on drunkenness with wine because of its reckless excess; the latter specifically contrasts drunkenness with being filled in the Spirit.

The prediction that a frequenter of prostitutes becomes poor corresponds to 29:3's statement that tending prostitutes destroys wealth; 23:21 includes drunkards and sleepy people in its warning as well.
The command not to despise a mother because she has grown old corresponds to 30:17's warning against the eye that dishonors a mother's old age and mocks a father.
The father's rejoicing over a wise son corresponds directly to 10:1's statement that a wise son makes his father glad.
The call for father and mother to rejoice over the child corresponds to 17:21's contrast between a father's lack of joy over an uneducated son and the intelligent son gladdening his mother.
Giving the heart and keeping the teacher's ways with one's eyes corresponds to 4:23-26's coordinated commands to guard the heart, direct the eyes toward righteousness and straighten one's tracks.
Proverbs 23:27 describes another's well as narrow alongside the leaking jar image of another's house; 9:18c likewise warns away from foreign water and drinking from a foreign spring.
The uproar, lawsuits and gratuitous bruises of 23:29, attributed to drinkers in its following verse, correspond to Sirach's description of excessive wine bringing conflict, anger and wounds.
The people lingering over wine and seeking drinking parties correspond to Isaiah's drinkers who pursue strong drink from morning into evening and neglect the Lord's works.
Both explicitly command against becoming drunk with wine; Proverbs then urges company with righteous people, while Ephesians directs being filled in the Spirit.

In the continuing portrait of the drinker, Proverbs pictures collapse and spreading poison like a snakebite; Sirach likewise warns that wine destroys many and that drunkenness diminishes strength and adds wounds.
The drinker's eyes on another woman and ensuing crooked words contrast with 4:24-25's commands to remove a crooked mouth and direct the eyes toward righteous things.
Proverbs compares the drinker's condition to a helmsman in heavy seas; the psalm conversely compares storm-tossed sailors' shaking and loss of wisdom to a drunken man.
After unperceived blows and mockery, the drinker plans to seek his companions again; 26:11 similarly pictures a fool returning to his wicked sin, compared there to a dog encountering its own vomit.
